name: Huitoto, Nüpode
confidence_why: Minor & Hendrich de Minor 1971 give first-syllable stress only as a general rule with many accent-marked exceptions, and Minor 1956, the sole phonological description of this dialect, treats stress with high pitch as a contrastive phoneme without any positional rule, so initial stress is a default rather than a strict rule and all the evidence comes from one fieldworker.
catalog_quote: Por regla general el acento de intensidad recae en la primera silaba de la palabra [in general an intensity accent is located on the first syllable of the word]. (Minor & Hendrich de Minor 1971:137) [...] There are many exceptions. Stress is accompanied by high pitch. (Minor 1956:137)

audit.recode_to: Not fixed-strict. reclassify as initial-default with lexically specified (phonemic) stress — i.e. not in the strict set, kind = the catalog's lexical/unpredictable-with-initial-default class (e.g. 'fixed-lax'/'lexical' per taxonomy), citing Minor 1956:137 ('complex suprasegmental phoneme of stress accompanied by high pitch') as deciding source and Minor & Minor 1971:137 as the orthographic default; note Wojtylak 2017:5 fn.2 ('only Murui and Mɨka have fixed accent position (word-initial). Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode appear to have different patterns of accent placement').
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page scan of the held 1971/2008 vocabulario, p.137. (2) But the classification 'fixed-strict initial' over-reads an orthographic convention: the same sentence says non-initial stress exists and is written with an accent, the same page prints jopóchupbi, atdáva, muìnánɨ, and sampled dictionary pages (pp.20, 30) show accent-marked non-initial stress on roughly half the polysyllabic headwords. (3) The primary phonology of this very dialect, Minor 1956 (downloaded now, open, page scan read), sets up stress+high pitch as a suprasegmental PHONEME and states no positional rule; its transcribed forms carry stress on varying syllables. StressTyp2's own passage already flagged 'many exceptions'. (4) Wojtylak 2017 (held), the current authority on Witoto, states that only Murui and Mɨka have fixed word-initial accent and that Nɨpode's accent placement differs. (5) No better
audit.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: re-verified on the page scan of the copy consulted, book p.137 = p.147 (Apéndice II 'Pronunciación y ortografía'): 'Por regla general el acento de intensidad recae en la primera sílaba de la palabra. Cuando no es así, se marca sobre la sílaba acentuada.' — verbatim; same page prints jopóchupbi 'casita', atdáva 'gallina' with marked non-initial stress. The second half of the record's the domain quotation ('There are many exceptions. Stress is accompanied by high pitch. (Minor 1956:137)') is a StressTyp2 compiler gloss: the downloaded IJAL scan

sources.quote: As a general rule the stress (intensity accent) falls on the first syllable of the word. When that is not the case, it is written over the stressed syllable.

sources.citation: Minor, Eugene E. 1956. Witoto vowel clusters. International Journal of American Linguistics 22(2): 131-137. doi:10.1086/464357 (Muinánɨ dialect, Ampiyacu River, Peru, fieldwork 1952-54).
sources.quote: 'The six vowel phonemes are i, e, a, o, u, ɨ. There is a complex suprasegmental phoneme of stress accompanied by high pitch.' Stress is treated as phonemic (contrastive); no positional rule is given anywhere in the article; cited forms show stress on the first syllable (hópo 'house', héiaɨ 'many rats', tékuai 'jump', áɨjue 'large') and on later syllables (uaiʔɨ́dɨkue 'I'm staying', daɨiñédikaɨ 'not like we are', makáoiakade p.131).
sources.note: The only phonological analysis of Nɨpode (same author, same Ampiyacu speakers as the 1971 vocabulario); it posits a stress PHONEME and gives no initial rule, so it should replace the orthography note as deciding source. downloaded now (open archive.org microfilm scan).

sources.quote: No statement on word stress or accent placement; instrumental study of vowel formants, duration, F0 and intensity at vowel midpoints only. §1.4 confirms prior Nɨpode-specific work is limited to Minor 1956, Minor & Minor and Griffiths (2000/2001, unpublished lexicon).

sources.citation: Wojtylak, Katarzyna Izabela. 2017. A grammar of Murui (Bue), a Witotoan language of Northwest Amazonia. PhD dissertation, James Cook University, Cairns. xxvi+611 pp. [published version: A Grammar of Murui (Bue), Brill 2020, doi:10.1163/9789004432673]
sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog huit1237). States that all Witoto dialects (Murui, Mɨka, Mɨnɨka, Nɨpode) lack tonal distinctions, like Nonuya and unlike Ocaina/Bora; only Murui and Mɨka have fixed word-initial accent, while Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode 'appear to have different patterns of accent placement', which led Ávila 2016 and Seifart & Fagua Rincón 2009 to hypothesize possible tonal contrasts in Mɨnɨka (not Nɨpode). Murui itself: stress word-initial, stressed/long vowels carry high pitch (§2.2-2.4).

tone.quote: Unlike other Witotoan languages, Murui is neither tonal, nor does it have a complex accent system. 2 ... [fn. 2] With regards to the lack of tonal distinction, all ‘Witoto’ dialects are similar to Nonuya but are unlike Ocaina and other languages of the People of the Centre cultural area. Note however that only Murui and Mɨka have fixed accent position (word-initial). Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode appear to have different patterns of accent placement. This has lead other researchers to hypothesize that it could possibly be indicative of tonal contrasts in Mɨnɨka (Ávila, 2016; Seifart & Fagua Rincón, 2009).
tone.locator: p. 4, §1.1 'Linguistic profile of Murui': the sentence 'Unlike other Witotoan languages, Murui is neither tonal..' and its footnote 2 are both on p. 4
tone.summary: No lexical tone in Nɨpode (per family-internal comparison); accent placement variable, not fixed initial.
tone.says: States that all Witoto dialects (Murui, Mɨka, Mɨnɨka, Nɨpode) lack tonal distinctions, like Nonuya and unlike Ocaina/Bora; only Murui and Mɨka have fixed word-initial accent, while Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode 'appear to have different patterns of accent placement', which led Ávila 2016 and Seifart & Fagua Rincón 2009 to hypothesize possible tonal contrasts in Mɨnɨka (not Nɨpode). Murui itself: stress word-initial, stressed/long vowels carry high pitch (§2.2-2.4).
